title: Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores
one_liner: Evidence packs showing a coarse satellite-derived wildfire score is wrong about one specific lot, filed under new statutory appeal rights.
customer: Independent insurance agents and HOAs or fire-safe councils in Colorado and California whose clients face nonrenewal or surcharges. Insurers' appeal desks are a later buyer.
problem: Colorado HB25-1182 (in force since July 1, 2026) makes insurers disclose the parcel's score, credit documented mitigation and offer an appeal. California AB 75, operative July 1, 2026, gives notice and dispute rights over aerial-imagery nonrenewals. But 'owners still have to prove their case', and many wildfire models lean on roughly 30 m fuel layers and stale imagery that misclassify irrigated, gravel-scaped or recently cleared lots.
solution: For each parcel, pull the disclosed model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density, distance to wildland) and overlay multi-date 15-50 cm satellite imagery showing vegetation change, roof material and clearance, plus dated homeowner photos. Produce a regulator-format rebuttal pack with a ranked list of cheap fixes, and give agents a dashboard that scans their whole book for likely score errors. The real edge is a growing database of which input errors insurers concede.
why_now: Both disclosure-and-appeal regimes went live in July 2026 and insurers' appeal desks are unprepared. Commercial constellations, including 30 cm Pelican and Vantor archives, plus 15 cm HD, have made high-resolution archives cheap. Regulators in CT, NH and PA say imagery alone is insufficient, and NY has a pending bill.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per parcel via agents. $10-$25 per parcel per year for HOA book scans. About $60 per appeal from insurers for standardised evidence intake.
non_obvious_insight: Wildfire scores are averages of coarse layers, so the cheapest way to change a score is often to fix an input error rather than harden the house. The resolution gap between 30 m models and 30 cm imagery is systematic, so a win on one lot tends to generalise to its neighbours and compounds into a book-level lever for agents.
first_30_days: Pick the Colorado Front Range. Recruit 5 independent agencies with 200+ WUI clients each, plus 2 HOAs. Run the first 50 score disclosures at a $99 pilot price per file, and track appeal success rate as the marketing asset.

title: Hours Exchange: Supply Side of the Work Requirement
one_liner: Invert the wallet: instead of helping people prove hours they already work, build the network of pre-certified nonprofit and public hosts that supply verifiable, flexible community-service and training hours, with insured hosts and signed hour records, paid per active member-month by health systems and plans.
customer: First buyer: population-health, community-benefit and Medicaid-strategy leads at nonprofit and county-owned safety-net health systems. Second buyer: plans. Supply side: 20-50 hosts per county, such as food banks and church pantries, school after-care, libraries, senior centers, community gardens, and clinics' own non-clinical roles. Members: the residual slice of expansion adults who are not exempt, not already working and need hours.
problem: Every product in the parent's competitor set assumes the hours exist and only tracks or verifies them (SteadyIQ, Emmy, the state tracking portals from Maximus, Optum and Acentra, Pointcare, Findhelp). For a member who lost a job or has no hours, no amount of documentation fixes anything. The IFR does count community service, work programs and combined activities toward the 80 hours a month, but there is no supply chain: hosts do not know the state verification standard, cannot supervise flexible 4-hour shifts, lack liability cover, and have no time to produce signed logs. A member 30 days from termination cannot find, book and verify 40 missing hours on their own.
solution: An activity marketplace with a verification rail. (1) Host certification: each host signs a one-page state-format verification protocol (who may sign, what is recorded, non-displacement pledge) and joins a registry that we pre-clear with the state Medicaid agency wherever possible. (2) Micro-shift board: hosts post 3-6 hour shifts (pantry Saturday 8-12), and members claim them by SMS in their language. (3) Verification: check-in and out by phone geofence or supervisor QR or SMS confirmation, producing tamper-evident hour records. (4) Monthly hours letter in the state's format, delivered to the member, the case file and the plan. (5) Master volunteer accident and liability policy plus background checks carried by us, which is the small balance-sheet element and a reason hosts join. (6) Guardrails: the flow starts with an exemption and already-compliant screen, so nobody who qualifies is routed to slots. Participation is voluntary. Later: the same hours count toward SNAP's parallel 80-hour rule (widened by the 2025 law; verify scope), TANF work participation, and court-ordered or scholarship service hours.
why_now: The requirement starts Jan 1, 2027, but the documentation phase is later (an HFMA summary of the IFR says self-attestation is allowed through 2027 and once per beneficiary in 2028). That makes 2027 the year to build the host registry and get states to accept it, before the paperwork wall. The first wave of notices will expose the supply gap, and first movers will hold the hosts and the state relationships. Health systems and plans need a measurable coverage-retention lever for community-benefit and health-related-social-needs spending. Cheap SMS, geofencing and LLM-drafted state-format letters make per-shift verification nearly free.
revenue_model: Health systems or plans pay $20-30 per active member-month (active means at least one verified shift that month). Pilot: about $40k for 150 members over 6 months at roughly $45 per member-month, including host onboarding. Illustrative unit economics: coordinator time $8-10, insurance about $1, SMS and verification about $1, for roughly 50% gross margin. Possible additional flows: SNAP E&T third-party reimbursement (50% federal match on eligible non-federal spending) for host costs where the state plan allows (verify eligibility of this activity), state workforce-board contracts, and later fees from courts and scholarship programs. Bottom-up ceiling, illustrative only: if 1 in 10 of the 2.3M projected FY27 coverage losers (per the HFMA/Applied Policy figure) needs slots, that is 230k people x $240 a year, about $55M a year before SNAP, TANF and court hours.
non_obvious_insight: For the residual slice, the constraint is not proof but the absence of qualifying, supervisable, flexible hours near the member's home. Hosts are short on labor and long on facilities, so this market clears cheaply for whoever supplies the insurance, verification and coordination. Second, a registry-verified, insured host is cheaper for a caseworker to trust than an individual's self-report. Once one state lists registry-verified hosts as accepted evidence, verification cost falls for everyone and the registry becomes the standard, with network economies (hosts and members) and a cornered resource (the state-acceptance record). That is the difference between a tool and infrastructure.
first_30_days: Pick one county in a state that verifies hours early. Ask the state Medicaid agency in writing what a community-service host must sign and record, and whether members can cure by showing current-month hours (the IFR summary says 30 days to demonstrate compliance; test whether that includes hours earned during the window). Get an LOI from one food-bank network covering 10 to 15 pantries as hosts, and quotes for a master volunteer accident policy. Run a manual pilot with 25 members from a clinic's at-risk list using a shared sheet and a Twilio number, and produce real hours letters. Have five conversations with health-system community-benefit leads and price a $40k, 6-month pilot. The 2027 honesty test: do hours letters raise state acceptance versus self-attestation alone?

title: Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers
one_liner: Validated dynamic load models and ride-through test packages so data centers can pass the same grid-code exams that generators pass.
customer: Interconnection teams at hyperscalers, neoclouds and colo developers, and their EPCs. Transmission owners and ISOs need the models validated, and the developer pays.
problem: About 1.5 GW of Northern Virginia data center load tripped offline together during a 2024 fault. AI training loads swing tens of MW in seconds, and xAI buys Megapacks largely to smooth them. Texas SB 6 and NERC large-load work now push for ride-through and dynamic models, but no standard model library or test lab exists for GPU cluster, power-supply and UPS stacks.
solution: Build a parametric EMT and PSS/E model library for common facility architectures (UPS topologies, PSU behavior, 800V DC). Validate it with hardware-in-the-loop tests at a partner lab. Sell per-project model packages, ride-through study reports and compliance-ready certification letters. Charge a subscription to keep models current as hardware changes.
why_now: Multi-GW campuses, NERC's large-load task force and Texas and PJM interconnection rules in 2025-26 are turning load models from optional into a gating item.
revenue_model: $75-300k per project for the model and study, an annual model-maintenance subscription, and test or certification fees paid by UPS and power-shelf OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames data centers as demand. The grid now treats them as a dynamic device, like a giant inverter-based generator. Inverter-generator modeling became a consulting industry after events like the 2016 Blue Cut fire, and large-load modeling will follow. The model library is the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit one or two power-electronics engineers from a utility or ISO. Publish an open primer on GPU-load oscillation. Contact interconnection leads at 10 neoclouds and 5 TO planners. Sell a $15k 'large-load model gap analysis'. Sign a university hardware-in-the-loop lab as a partner.

title: Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities
one_liner: A fee-based 'is this data center developer real?' diligence service for electric co-ops and municipal utilities drowning in 100-1,000 MW inquiries from shell LLCs.
customer: G&T and distribution electric cooperatives, municipal utilities and PUDs (5-person engineering staffs, no data center experience). Secondary: state economic development offices and county governments granting abatements. The utility or its G&T pays per inquiry or on retainer.
problem: Every small utility with transmission access is now getting inquiries for 200-1,000 MW campuses from LLCs formed 90 days ago. Each one eats study money, planning time and political capital, and a wrong bet strands ratepayer-funded infrastructure. Texas's proposed SB 6 rule (16 TAC 25.194, final rule due by end of 2026) would require $50,000/MW of financial security before a study and disclosure of duplicate requests. That pushes speculators into neighboring states and co-ops with softer tariffs. Small utilities have no way to tell a real project from a PowerPoint.
solution: A standardized 12-point 'physical reality' test built from paper trails that real projects leave and phantom ones cannot. (1) Air permit applications for generators, where the genset count implies the MW. (2) An OEM order acknowledgment or slot reservation for MV transformers and switchgear, plus a delivery date that fits the claimed energization date. (3) Recorded site control (deed or option). (4) Water and stormwater filings. (5) A named tenant LOI or offtaker. (6) A GC or EPC that has actually built a campus. (7) A financing letter. (8) Tax-abatement filings. (9) LLC principals cross-checked against other states' filings, to catch the same MW shopped to five utilities. (10) A power-density and cooling design consistent with the load ask. (11) Local land-use posture. (12) Team track record. The deliverable is a red/amber/green memo, a recommended security amount, and a milestone-gated study structure the utility can put in its ESA. Add-ons are a large-load tariff and ESA term-sheet template and a duplicate-request registry that co-ops in a region can pool.
why_now: Large-load tariffs and collateral rules are landing right now: Texas SB 6 (signed June 2025, PUCT rule proposed March 2026, final expected by 12/31/2026), plus AEP Ohio-style minimum-demand tariffs. Each new collateral regime displaces phantom load to the next-weakest utility. Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 mean that a real project without an equipment slot is not real, which gives a very cheap and reliable test. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or canceled, so utilities are burned and skeptical.
revenue_model: $7.5K-25K per inquiry vetting memo; $60K-150K/yr retainers for G&T co-ops that field 10+ inquiries a year; $25K-50K one-time tariff/ESA template packages; later a subscription to a multi-utility duplicate-request registry. Utilities can often pass the cost to the applicant as a study-deposit line item.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think the hard part of large-load planning is forecasting demand. Insiders know real projects are betrayed by equipment, not slides. A serious 300 MW developer has a transformer slot, a generator count on an air permit and a GC on payroll before the utility ever hears the name. A phantom has none of those. The tell is the logistics trail, and nobody at a 5-person co-op knows where to look. Texas's high collateral will also export the phantom problem to everyone else.
first_30_days: Build scrapers for state air-permit databases in 6-8 states and county deed/LLC records for 3 co-op service territories. Ask 3 co-op contacts (via state electric cooperative associations or a G&T's planning group) for their last 10 inquiries and run free back-tests on how they turned out. Publish a one-page '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' on LinkedIn and co-op association channels. Convert the first 2-3 into paid $7.5K memos on live inquiries and ask for a G&T retainer.

Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.

The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.

- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.

title: Ride-Through Witness: Measure-First Large-Load Network
one_liner: Invert the parent's model-before-energization: ingest the UPS logs and power-quality waveforms sites already record, join them with grid-side PMU data, and auto-produce ISO-format ride-through and oscillation reports, growing into the reference data network that ISOs, OEMs and insurers rely on.
customer: Wedge: reliability and compliance managers and facility engineering leads at operators of 25-200 MW neocloud and colo sites in ERCOT and PJM, already energized or energizing. Second-side payers later are ISOs and TOs (aggregate feeds and model-validation reports), UPS and power-shelf OEMs (fleet analytics), and insurers.
problem: When a grid fault drops hundreds of MW of data center load, the ISO asks every site whether it tripped and why. The evidence sits inside the facility: UPS event logs, PQ-meter waveforms, power-shelf telemetry and transfer-to-backup thresholds. ISO PMUs only see the outside. As I read the reported 2024 Northern Virginia loss of about 1.5 GW, its cause was facility-side protection and backup-transfer behavior that grid operators could not see (verify against the NERC incident review). Pre-energization models are never validated against reality, and they decay as GPU firmware and UPS settings change monthly. Operators face blame, curtailment and NOGRR282 exposure with no forensic evidence and no ride-through margin figure.
solution: Software-first, with no hardware in the first release. 'Witness' ingests existing data (UPS event logs, PQDIF and COMTRADE files from existing PQ meters and relays, generator and BESS logs) and time-aligns it with public ISO and PMU frequency data. Within 24 hours of any event it generates an ISO-format disturbance report: what tripped, at what threshold and delay, how fast load recovered, and the oscillation signature. It also runs a continuous dashboard against NOGRR282 thresholds and detects GPU-cluster synchronized swings. Phase 2 adds a white-label certified point-on-wave recorder for sites without one. Phase 3 turns fleet data into measurement-validated models, a model-versus-reality score, OEM firmware benchmarks and an insurance risk score. We offer the report schema to ISOs and NERC as a standard, the equivalent of the IBR event-analysis and monitoring standards (PRC-028/029/030).
why_now: NOGRR282 has been in force since Aug 1, 2026, so the industry moves from modeling to operations, and the first real ride-through events at AI sites are being recorded now. NERC's IBR standards (PRC-028/029/030) show the regulatory template of monitoring plus event analysis for inverter-based resources, and it is plausible to extend it to large loads (unverified). GPU-load oscillation is now a public concern. Every operator already logs the data, and cheap cloud compute plus LLM-assisted log parsing make ingesting heterogeneous vendor formats cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: Operators: $30-70k per site per year for the subscription, or $10-15k per retro-analysis or event report. ISOs and TOs: $100-500k per year each for aggregated feeds and model-validation reports once 30 or more sites are connected. OEMs: $50-200k per year for cross-brand fleet analytics. Insurers: risk-score licensing. Data network effects and standard-setting are what make this a 10x outcome, with 300 sites at $50k as $15M in operator revenue alone, plus roughly the same again from the other sides.
non_obvious_insight: The 2024 event was an inside-the-facility information problem, and only the join of facility recorders and grid PMUs establishes causation. No single site sees aggregate risk, and only a neutral third party can pool data across UPS brands and operators, which OEMs and hyperscalers will not. That gives network economies and a cornered resource, proprietary as-measured behavior of real AI facilities in real faults. The parent sells the exam and this sells the proof you keep passing it. Free generic models cannot substitute for a fleet-wide, as-measured dataset. A retro-analysis of an operator's own past voltage dips is a sellable product with no OEM or pre-energization model required.
first_30_days: Sell a $10-15k Ride-Through Margin Audit built from an operator's own historical voltage-dip and UPS-transfer events, delivered by hand as a concierge service. Recruit one power-quality or protection engineer and one data engineer. Build parsers for PQDIF, COMTRADE and two or three UPS log formats. Contact reliability and compliance leads at 20 operators (ERCOT and PJM) and 3 TO or ISO planners, and offer a free report on one public event to each. Publish the draft report schema and an open primer on GPU oscillation signatures. Confirm what NOGRR282 requires in terms of operations-phase reporting.

title: Megawatt Credit Bureau with Bonded Collateral
one_liner: Invert the vetting desk: real developers pay to be rated, utilities accept the rating for lower deposits, and the company eventually underwrites large-load security bonds off the physical-readiness data, so regulators' collateral rules become the market instead of the threat.
customer: First payer: mid-size and regional developers with real sites and real equipment slots (powered-land developers, ex-bitcoin-miner sites converting to AI, regional colo builders) that are in 10-30 utility queues and being asked for $50K/MW collateral or up to $100K per study in each. Accepting side: co-op and municipal pools that agree to recognize the rating. Capital side: a specialty surety or insurance carrier and reinsurer that provide bond capacity through an MGA structure.
problem: Collateral regimes (Texas proposes $50K/MW, AEP Ohio-style deposits) treat every applicant as a phantom. A real 300 MW project must lock up $15M in cash or letters of credit per utility, and re-submit the same package to each co-op. Hyperscaler-backed developers have the balance sheet and shells do not, so thinly capitalized developers with real projects get squeezed or forced to sell to bigger players. Surety and LC markets price the principal's balance sheet, not the project's physical readiness, so there is no credit signal between a hyperscaler guarantee and a shell LLC. Utilities cannot tell the difference either.
solution: Phase 1 (months 0-6): the 'Verified Ready' dossier for $15-25K. The developer hands over what real projects have (air permit, deed or option, OEM slot confirmation, EPC contract, tenant LOI, financing letter), and the desk verifies it through public records and direct confirmation calls. It issues a dated, registry-anchored readiness rating (R1-R5) that pilot co-op pools accept as satisfying Gates 0-1 and as grounds for a 30-50% deposit reduction or study priority. Utilities pay nothing. Phase 2 (months 6-18): a bonded-collateral program, meaning surety-style 'large-load security bonds' written by a specialty carrier through an MGA, priced off the rating and posted to the utility as obligee in place of part of the cash or LC collateral. Phase 3: publish the methodology as an open standard and lobby tariffs and regulators to reference it, e.g. 'rated applicants may post bonds or reduced collateral.' The registry accumulates milestone-hit data on who actually energizes, which becomes proprietary loss data no one else has.

Transformer lead times of 3-5 years and switchgear sold out into 2028 make equipment evidence a cheap, hard-to-fake readiness signal that a rating can be built on. The paying base self-selects to real projects because phantoms will not pay to be scrutinized. The classic conflict of interest of issuer-paid ratings is solved by having the MGA and carrier carry loss exposure, so the rater has skin in the game, unlike a ratings shop. title: Tariff Surcharge Clawback for B2B Buyers
one_liner: A contingency-fee service that mines a buyer's 2025-26 supplier invoices for 'tariff surcharge' lines and recovers a share of the IEEPA refunds those suppliers are now collecting.
customer: Multi-unit restaurant and retail franchisees, contractor purchasing co-ops, and mid-market distributors' customers that paid itemized tariff, freight or 'inflation' surcharges to suppliers who were the importer of record. They pay a 20-30% success fee on money recovered.
problem: IEEPA duty refunds go only to the importer of record (IOR) or a party the IOR designates. Buyers who paid the tariff as a surcharge or a higher price get nothing unless they ask. AutoZone booked about $96M and Cracker Barrel $15M, with MillerKnoll $16.5M and Worthington $4M. Downstream buyers have no visibility into what their suppliers recovered and no process to ask for it.
solution: Read-only inbox and AP connectors pull 2025-26 invoices and extract surcharge, 'tariff', 'duty' and 'trade cost recovery' line items. The system estimates each supplier's IEEPA exposure from public import-manifest data. It checks the supplier's terms for pass-back language, such as 'surcharge will be removed or refunded if tariffs are rescinded'. It then generates a claim letter with an offer to accept credit memos or to have the supplier name the buyer as the CBP Form 4811 notify party so the refund routes to the buyer. A second module audits new diesel and fuel surcharges against the contract formula and the EIA diesel index. Claims are sent to the top 20 suppliers per buyer, and unclaimed money is tracked to closure.
why_now: CBP's CAPE portal opened in 2026 and is issuing refunds within 60-90 days of an accepted declaration. Refunds are landing in Q3-Q4 2026 P&Ls as one-time gains. Suppliers are least defensible in the first months after booking a windfall and will negotiate to keep customer goodwill. Diesel is $6.53/gal, up $2.78 year over year, so a wave of fresh surcharge invoices is arriving that nobody audits.
revenue_model: A 20-30% contingency fee on recovered refunds and credits, plus $199-$999/month for continuous surcharge auditing (fuel, energy, 'regulatory recovery' fees) once the first recovery lands.
non_obvious_insight: The refund windfall is a transfer from customers to importers, and the CFOs say so. AutoZone's CFO said 'the refund environment was deflationary, and the industry likely would have raised prices faster if both retailers and suppliers hadn't received cost relief' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/autozone-azo-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Cracker Barrel booked a $15M refund and MillerKnoll $16.5M, worth 180 bps of gross margin (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/cracker-barrel-cbrl-q4-2026-earnings-call-transcript/ and https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/22/mlkn-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). CBP states 'Only the IOR ... or the authorized customs broker ... may file' and never mentions downstream buyers, couriers or DDP shipments (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds). Every downstream claim is therefore a negotiation, and the buyer who holds the 2025 invoices has the leverage. Nobody is selling that to the buyer side. The legal caveat is that the buyer needs an explicit surcharge line or contract language to have a real claim, so the product should target only those cases.
first_30_days: Recruit 5-8 restaurant franchisee groups or contractor purchasing co-ops through franchisee associations and buying-group managers, with a free 'we only get paid if you get paid' offer. Export 2025 AP data or forward invoice PDFs, then have an analyst plus an LLM extraction script build a surcharge ledger for the top 15 suppliers each. Send the first 30 claim letters with a one-page template that cites the refund program and asks for credit or 4811 routing. Have a supply-chain lawyer review the template. Aim to close the first paid recovery within 60-75 days.

title: Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Give pet insurers the claim-edit engine human health has had for 30 years: canonical procedure codes, bundling rules, and price benchmarks for messy vet invoices.
customer: Pet insurance MGAs, carriers and TPAs adjudicating roughly 100k to 2M claims a year, the mid-size players without in-house claims data science. Later, corporate veterinary groups and pet-owner pre-treatment estimate checks.
problem: Veterinary invoices are free-text line items exported from practice-management systems, with no universal procedure code set and no NCCI-style edits. Adjusters hand-review them. Insurers cannot tell that the vet billed anesthesia monitoring, an IV catheter, fluids and the e-collar as separate lines on top of a surgery fee, or what a routine dental cleaning costs in a given ZIP code. Claim severity is inflating with vet consolidation, and insurers answer with blanket premium hikes instead of line-level accuracy.
solution: An API that ingests invoice PDFs or line items. An LLM plus a hand-built taxonomy of the top ~300 vet procedures (about 80% of spend) normalizes each line to a canonical code. A rules layer, built the way NCCI and medically-unlikely edits work, flags unbundling, duplicates and implausible units. A benchmark layer returns usual-and-customary ranges by ZIP and practice type. The adjuster sees pay, reduce or review, with reason codes.
why_now: There are roughly 7 million insured US pets, and the segment is growing at double-digit rates with loss-ratio and price-hike pressure. Corporate vet consolidation is raising invoice complexity. LLMs make invoice line-item normalization, the hard part that took human-health edit vendors years, cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Per-claim fee of $0.25-$0.75, or 10-15% of validated savings. A 500k-claim MGA is worth $150-350k a year. Add a benchmark-data license for vet chains and an owner-facing estimate checker later.
non_obvious_insight: Every automation wave in healthcare billing started with standardized codes and claim edits, not with AI. Cotiviti and Optum are basically edit libraries with sales teams. Pet insurance is at the pre-CPT stage. Someone who has spent years living inside code sets, bundling logic and 'this is included in the global fee' arguments can build the missing layer in weeks. Insurers will not fund a fight with vets. They will fund a neutral, consistent, explainable edit that does not vary by adjuster.
first_30_days: Recruit one ex-coder (CPC) and a vet tech consultant. Build the 300-line taxonomy from public estimate sheets and a few hundred sample invoices. Approach 10 pet-insurance MGAs and TPAs with a free retrospective: run 5,000 of their anonymized past invoices and report the dollar share found in bundled, duplicate or out-of-range lines. Convert the best result into a paid pilot on per-claim pricing.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

Pet insurers have no contracts with vets and no 'global fee' concept, and they pay owners by reimbursement. Line-level reductions therefore land on policyholders as balance bills, which invites complaints and regulatory attention. I found no US insurer RFP or public spend for this. The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany.

title: Orphan Lien Clearance Desk for Title Agents
one_liner: A flat-fee curative service that proves dead solar fixture filings and other zombie liens are dead (or gets them released) so home closings stop stalling.
customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and real estate attorneys in high-solar states (AZ, CA, FL, TX, NJ, NC, NV, CO), billed per file and usually paid by the seller at closing. Listing agents in solar-heavy markets are a second channel.
problem: Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 (500,000+ customers), Mosaic and PosiGen followed, and the residential solar credit ended for 2026 installs, so thousands of homes carry UCC-1 fixture filings and recorded solar-lease notices held by dead, merged or reassigned entities. Title examiners flag every one. Agents can't tell who holds the debt now, whether the filing is even still legally effective, or how to get a termination, so closings slip days or weeks. The people currently serving this are consumer SEO and lead-gen sites, not the title agents who actually need it solved on a deadline.
solution: Per-file lien autopsy delivered in 48 hours. (1) Pull the recorded instrument and any continuation or termination filings from the county index and the Secretary of State. (2) Compute lapse under UCC 9-515 (five years unless continued in the six-month window). (3) Trace the assignment and servicer chain through bankruptcy dockets and servicer notices. (4) Deliver either an underwriter-ready 'lapsed, no exception' memo, or a payoff/estoppel request plus a pre-drafted termination (UCC-3, or debtor-filed termination where the statute allows) recorded in that county's required format. Recorded memoranda of lease, which do not lapse, get a release workflow instead. Later expand the same engine to satisfied-but-never-released mortgages, expired judgment liens, dead PACE liens and resurfaced zombie second mortgages.
why_now: 2025-2026 solar installer bankruptcies (Sunnova, Mosaic, PosiGen) and the end of the residential solar credit produced the largest single wave of orphaned fixture filings ever recorded. 2018-2021 installs are now hitting their five-year lapse dates just as those homes come to market. Title agents are short-staffed and want to outsource curative work, and an LLM can read county index entries and bankruptcy docket text cheaply.
revenue_model: Flat fee of about $395-$900 per cleared file, contingent on clear-to-close. Agencies with volume pay $299/month plus a reduced per-file rate. White-label API for underwriters and closing software later.
non_obvious_insight: Half the 'problem liens' in solar-heavy counties are already legally dead, but the county index never shows lapse, so examiners treat a 2019 fixture filing as live forever. Clerks watch continuation filings come in, and most small installers never filed one. The work is proof of death, not payoff. Insiders also know the recorded 'notice of lease' is a different animal that never lapses, and that a clerk must record a debtor-filed termination on its face, since the office is ministerial.
first_30_days: Offer the first five files free to 3-5 independent title agencies in Phoenix, Tampa and Sacramento. Build the lapse calculator and county-index lookups for about 10 counties. Get one regional agent underwriter to accept a standard lapse-memo format. Then price at $495 per file and ask each agency for a testimonial and two referrals to listing agents.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SunStrong Management (successor servicer for the Sunnova book), Wolters Kluwer Lien Solutions / CSC (UCC search, filing, continuation and termination vendors), Qualia (title/escrow closing platform), Nationwide Title Clearing / national title-clearing and lien-release outsourcers (ServiceLink, etc.). White space: Research limits: the session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted, so I ran no searches. I used direct fetches of known URLs (Wikipedia, Cornell LII for the UCC text, SunStrong, Sunnova, Qualia, TitleCapture, Simplifile, the YC directory) and a GitHub repo search. Several guessed URLs 404'd or returned 403. Competitor coverage is therefore thin, and I found no funded startup doing solar-specific lien-lapse analysis and curative for title agents. Absence in my results is weak evidence, not proof.

Unserved as far as I could tell: a title-agent-facing, per-file workflow that (a) classifies the instrument (UCC-1 fixture filing vs. SOS-only filing vs. recorded memorandum or notice of lease vs. PACE vs. mortgage), (b) computes lapse under UCC 9-515, and (c) routes the file to the current servicer with a pre-formatted payoff, estoppel or UCC-3 request. Incumbent UCC vendors and general title-clearing outsourcers do not appear to package this for solar.

Substantive weaknesses to weigh against the gap:
- Lapse is not death. Cornell LII (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-515) confirms that on lapse the interest becomes unperfected, and is deemed never perfected only as against a purchaser for value. The debt and the interest against the debtor survive. In a lease or PPA the lessor owns the equipment, so a lapse memo does not clear ownership or the lease. The buyer still needs an assumption or buyout. Underwriters may therefore refuse to rely on 'lapsed, no exception' memos, and getting one to accept a format is the make-or-break step.
- Debtor-filed terminations are narrow. UCC 9-509(d)(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-509) requires the secured party to have failed to comply with 9-513, plus debtor authorization and a statement on the form. That generally means a demand and a wait, and it only works where no obligation is still secured. That conflicts with a 48-hour SLA.
- The 'orphan' premise is overstated for Sunnova, the biggest name. Its assets went to new owners and SunStrong runs a home-sale transfer process. The truly orphaned pool (Mosaic, PosiGen, small defunct installers) is smaller and messier. Sunnova is confirmed only via Wikipedia and the SunStrong and Sunnova sites. I could not fetch a Mosaic or PosiGen page.
- Unauthorized-practice-of-law exposure for underwriter-facing lapse opinions unless an attorney of record signs.
- Per-county recording quirks make it operations-heavy, not pure software.

title: Herd Roll-Forward: Lender-Paid Cattle Collateral Reconciliation
one_liner: Sell ag lenders a loan covenant that rebuilds the borrower's herd from paper that third parties generated (vet records, sale-barn settlements, brand certificates, tag and vaccine purchases) and flags loans where expected head and claimed head do not reconcile.
customer: Wedge: the chief credit officer and senior ag lender at one Farm Credit association or one $500M-$3B community bank in a brand-inspection state (Nebraska, South Dakota, Montana, Wyoming or the Texas Panhandle). It should carry $50M+ in cow-calf, bred-heifer and heifer-development loans of $500K-$5M. The bank pays, and the cost passes through to the borrower as a collateral inspection fee that lenders already charge. The vet is a paid data source, not the customer.
problem: The parent's own flaws are the problem to fix. A borrower-initiated count means fraudulent borrowers never opt in. A chute-side count proves only what was at the chute that day, not cattle on other leases, cattle sold since, or cattle double-pledged. It says nothing about ownership or lien priority. Vets may refuse to sign anything that reads as a collateral audit. And $2-3/head split with the vet is thin. Meanwhile lenders still rely on drive-by counts and borrower spreadsheets on loans where a 500-cow herd is $1.5M+ of collateral nobody independent has counted.
solution: An annual 'Herd Roll-Forward' per loan that closes an inventory equation: last year's verified head + expected calf crop (from preg-check records) + purchases (sale-barn buyer settlements, health certificates) - sales (consignor settlements, brand and feedyard closeouts) - deaths = expected ending head. That figure is compared with the borrower's claimed head and any chute-side scan. A second check triangulates consumables: EID tags bought, vaccine doses and dewormer from the vet, mineral and hay purchases, and grazing-lease animal-unit-months, all versus claimed head. The borrower signs one information-rights rider at loan closing, which lets the vet, sale barns, brand agency and feed suppliers release records to us. That rider is what removes adverse selection: the loan agreement opts the borrower in, not the borrower. LLM extraction reads the messy PDFs and photos. The vet is one attestor, contracted narrowly ('I handled N head with these IDs on this date', no collateral opinion) and paid a flat $150-300 per session for exporting the sheet they already made and one-tap signing. The lender gets a variance flag, a lien and ownership panel (UCC or state central-filing search plus brand records) and a portfolio dashboard.
why_now: (1) Reading hundreds of differently formatted settlement statements, invoices and health papers used to take an analyst hours per loan, and LLM document extraction has cut that to cents. That is the cost-stack collapse that makes reconciliation cheaper than a drive-by. (2) Federal EID tag rules for many interstate cattle movements (Nov 2024) mean more animals carry digital IDs and more vets and barns hold exportable records. (3) Record cattle prices are pushing herd rebuilding onto debt, with bred cows around $3,000+, so each loan carries big collateral. Lenders are also carrying delinquencies, and a fresh cattle-collateral fraud case (claimed in the parent, unverified) is prompting loan-committee questions. (4) It is fall, when preg-checks, weaning and calf sales generate the documents, and December-February annual renewals are when banks decide on inspections.
revenue_model: The bank pays per loan per year: about $600 under $1M, $1,500 for $1-3M and $3,000 above $3M, roughly 5-10 bps of balance. A portfolio dashboard is $1,000-2,000/month at 100+ loans. A bank with 120 cattle loans is worth about $130K-180K/yr. Vets get a flat per-session data fee, so their cost does not scale with head count. Target gross margin is 70%+ once extraction is automated, with human review only on flagged loans. Later add anonymized county and herd-size variance benchmarks for credit committees and examiners.
non_obvious_insight: Do not count the cattle, count the paper. Every animal movement leaves a record in a third party's hands (barn, brand inspector, vet, feed store, feedyard), and fraud shows up as arithmetic that does not close. Counting heads is the least informative check, so the chute day is a calibration anchor rather than the product. This also makes the vet's reluctance irrelevant, since any attestor or document set works, and it turns the borrower's own suppliers into the fraud detectors.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: run 12 interviews (5 loan officers or credit officers, 3 vets, 2 barn clerks, 2 brand inspectors). Ask each bank who does its inspections now and what it costs, and search for existing third-party collateral inspectors. Weeks 2-3: get one bank to pick 15 existing borrowers up for renewal and get consent. Manually reconcile each from documents the borrower already holds (sale settlements, preg-check sheets, vet invoices, tag orders) and from one vet's exports. Charge $500 per loan, or waive the fee for the first five if the bank agrees to write down what it learned. Week 4: present the variance results to the bank's ag loan committee, especially any loan that did not close. Convert the result into a one-page 'inventory information rights' rider for new bred-heifer and operating-line loans, priced at $750-1,500 per loan.

title: Interim Smoke-Damage Protocol Before the State Standard
one_liner: Publish and run the defensible smoke, ash and soot assessment protocol that California insurers, adjusters and lawyers will need on January 1, 2027, because the official technical standard will not exist until 2028-2029.
customer: California carriers, the FAIR Plan and their TPAs (for AB 1795's 30-day inspection and testing obligations), plus public adjusters, policyholder attorneys, and escrow, lender and buyer parties in standing-home sales. Homeowners pay via their insurer, PA or directly.
problem: California signed AB 1795 and AB 1642 on Sept 15, 2026. From Jan 1, 2027, insurers must inspect within 30 days, pay for necessary testing, keep paying ALE until restoration, and face a presumption that ash, soot and char in a standing home are fire-caused. But the state toxics department will not finish lead and asbestos standards until end of 2028 and other contaminant standards until 2029. Meanwhile tens of thousands of claims will need a protocol that survives litigation; existing vendor assessments are already accused of being substandard, and capacity of qualified industrial hygienists is scarce and expensive.
solution: An independent, openly published interim assessment protocol built on existing standards (IICRC S700, established sampling and lab methods, EPA/HUD dust-wipe criteria), developed with certified industrial hygienists and a toxicologist. Delivered as a product: a sampling-plan generator (which rooms, surfaces and ducts, how many samples), a trained technician network with kits and a chain-of-custody app, remote IH sign-off, a lab partner, a compliance-clock dashboard for carriers, and a 'smoke clearance certificate' for resale and escrow. Priced at a fraction of full CIH scopes.
why_now: The laws were signed two weeks ago with an effective date of Jan 1, 2027, LA County is investigating Farmers over Eaton/Palisades claim denials, a proposed class action targets vendor assessments, and carriers oppose but must comply. The gap between the compliance date and the state standard is a 2-3 year window in which the best-documented protocol becomes the de facto reference, and other fire states (Colorado, Oregon, Hawaii) are watching.
revenue_model: Per-home assessment of $1,800-$4,500 (paid by insurer under AB 1795 or the policyholder), $500 clearance-certificate add-on, lab pass-through margin, SaaS compliance dashboard for carriers at $2-$5 per claim per month, and training and certification fees for restoration technicians.
non_obvious_insight: In smoke disputes the lab is rarely the fight; the fight is the sampling design and the pass/fail threshold. Carriers whose vendors sample five spots and compare against urban background dust get 'clean' results by construction. Whoever publishes a transparent, replicable sampling grid with chain of custody writes the eventual standard, because regulators borrow the protocol with the most field data.
first_30_days: Recruit two CIHs and one toxicologist as an advisory board and draft 'Interim Smoke Assessment Protocol v0.1' for public comment. Train 6-10 IICRC-certified restoration technicians and buy sampling kits. Sell 20 pilot assessments in Altadena and Palisades at a subsidized $950 through public adjusters and attorneys, gathering data and case studies. Pitch 3 carriers and 2 TPAs on 30-day compliance capacity before January 1, offering a pilot at cost in exchange for using the protocol.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven.

title: Phantom Pipeline Audits for Utility Rate-Case Intervenors
one_liner: Sell to the ratepayers who pay for phantom load, meaning industrial customer groups and state consumer advocates in IRP, CPCN and large-load-tariff dockets, a testimony-ready audit of how much of a utility's confidential data-center pipeline is physically real.
customer: Buyer: counsel and expert budgets of (a) industrial customer intervenor groups (steel, paper, chemicals) that fear being left with stranded data-center infrastructure costs, and (b) state consumer advocate offices, in dockets where the utility's generation or transmission request rests on a data-center pipeline. Later: county and city governments facing abatement votes ($15-30K packs), and utility credit and equity analysts who subscribe to a Phantom Ratio Index. The sales path is through the law firms and staff attorneys who run these dockets.
problem: Utilities are asking commissions to approve gigawatts of gas plants and transmission justified by 'signed' large-load pipelines. The pipeline exhibits are confidential or anonymized ('Customer A, 400 MW'). Intervenor experts can only critique them top-down with econometrics, because nobody checks entries one by one against the physical trail. The evidence that pipelines are inflated is broad: an EPRI survey found none of 10 utilities with requests of 50%+ of peak expected actual 5-year load above 35% of peak, and Exelon's estimates fell about 40% after stricter collateral. But the intervenor cannot show which megawatts are fake, and a project shopped to two utilities is counted twice.
solution: A 'realization audit' delivered through counsel. Under the docket's protective order, the desk takes the utility's pipeline exhibit (MW, county or substation, in-service date, status). It scores each entry against the public trail: air permits and generator counts, deed or option and rezoning agenda items, water and stormwater filings, principal and LLC cross-matching across states, and whether the claimed in-service date is feasible given published equipment lead times. The output is a probability-weighted realized MW by year with confidence bands, a list of duplicate-counted megawatts across utilities, and a testimony-ready exhibit sponsored by a credentialed expert witness (a retired utility planner or former commission staffer on retainer). Where entries are fully anonymized, the audit triangulates from county-level permit and land-use activity and asks the commission to compel the identities under protective order. The same work product seeds a quarterly Phantom Ratio Index by utility and state.
why_now: Electricity affordability is a live political issue in the November 2026 midterms, and data-center load forecasts are the key contested input in a wave of 2026 large-load tariff, IRP and generation-certificate dockets. Regulators are already moving on transparency (Texas ownership audit, Pennsylvania's Aug 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW), so intervenors now have standing to ask for pipeline detail. Cleanview-style permit trackers plus OCR'd county records have made the public-trail checks cheap enough to run per docket at a fixed fee.
revenue_model: $40-120K fixed fee per docket engagement, covering the audit, exhibit and expert sponsorship, paid from intervenor budgets and industrial group dues. $15-30K county and municipal packs. A $25-60K/yr Phantom Ratio Index seat for credit analysts, muni and equity desks and hedge funds. Year-1 target: 6-10 dockets ($600K-$900K) plus early index subscribers, with about 60% gross margin because the expert and analyst time is billable.
non_obvious_insight: The parties who lose most from phantom load are not the utility's five planners but the other ratepayers, and they already have lawyers, a procedural calendar and an expert budget. The docket schedule sets the deadline, so no procurement cycle is needed. The natural competitors, utility-aligned engineering consultancies, are conflicted when the audit target is their client's pipeline, which makes an adversarial audit counter-positioned rather than just different. And duplicate-counting is only visible from outside: each utility sees only its own queue, but an auditor working in four states sees the same project in three pipelines. The adversarial work therefore seeds the national duplicate registry from a side no utility-aligned vendor can reach.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every live docket in 6-8 states where a large-load pipeline is in dispute, using public commission dockets, and note testimony deadlines in the next 60-120 days plus who the intervenors and their counsel are. Days 10-20: build a free 2-page 'public trail check' of one utility's publicly disclosed data-center announcements, using licensed permit data plus deeds and permits, and send it to 15 intervenor counsel and consumer advocate staff. Recruit a credentialed expert witness (retired planner or ex-commission staff). Days 20-30: close 1-2 paid engagements at about $40K, one with an industrial group and one with a consumer advocate. Kill test: if counsel will not pay $40K for a per-entry audit because their econometric expert already covers it, the intervenor thesis is dead and the index is the fallback.
lineage: mutation of I0079 ('Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check. | How this version avoids them: GridUnity, PowerClerk, Camus and Ascend sell software to utilities as vendors, run on applicant-supplied data and cannot be adversarial. Enverus (load forecasting for utilities), LandGate and GridCARE serve utilities or developers. Cleanview is a free tracker with no per-entry audit, expert witness or confidential pipeline access, so it is a data input, not a rival. ZEG advises developers and utilities. NRECA serves co-ops and has nothing for IOU dockets. Utility-aligned consultancies (Burns & McDonnell and similar) are conflicted by their clients, and existing intervenor-side experts do top-down forecast critique, not entry-level physical-trail verification. The buyer, the payer and the deliverable are all different from the parent's co-op memo, so nobody in the parent's research is selling to the same person.

title: Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers
one_liner: Take the workfile custody, E&O tail worry and direct lender clients off retiring appraisers, then hand the practice to supervised trainees, a bridge the industry has never had.
customer: Certified residential appraisers about 58 and older deciding whether to learn the new UAD 3.6 workflow or quit pay $1,500-2,500 one-time. Successor side: credit unions, community banks and attorneys with direct-relationship orders pay recurring fees. Career-changers (agents, inspectors, adjusters, contractors) become trainees under our supervisors.
problem: An appraisal practice has no sale value. The license is personal and the AMC clients aren't transferable. Retirement is also frightening. USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (longer with litigation). E&O claims can arrive years later, so a costly tail policy is needed. Board complaints and subpoenas don't stop. Meanwhile UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 with new forms and data, which is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. The active workforce has reportedly shrunk from over 90,000 (2016) to about 65,000, and rural counties lose their only appraiser.
solution: (1) Secure digital workfile custody with retrieval, subpoena and board-inquiry response, and a group E&O tail program (brokerage commission). (2) A recorded 3-hour 'local knowledge' interview plus the retiree's adjustment grids and neighborhood boundary notes, packaged into a playbook for the successor. (3) Successor placement: trainees under a certified supervisor of record (the retiree part-time for 12-24 months on a stipend and earn-out, or another certified appraiser), with desk-review and AI QC before signature. (4) The retiree's direct lender clients move to the successor with a personal handoff.
why_now: UAD 3.6 is mandatory for new GSE submissions from Nov 2, 2026. The AQB's second exposure draft (comments closed Aug 30, 2026) proposes removing the college-degree requirement and experience-timeline barriers, which widens the trainee pool. Executive Order 14393 (March 2026) directs regulators to simplify appraiser qualifications and expand alternative valuations. The rural shortage is acute and lenders want reliable local coverage.
revenue_model: $1,800 one-time custody plus transition package, or about $29/month for archive-only. E&O tail brokerage commissions. A 15-25% earn-out on inherited direct-client revenue for 24 months. 20-30% of trainee-produced fee revenue for QC and supervisor-of-record services. Coverage-guarantee contracts with rural credit unions and community banks.
non_obvious_insight: The asset isn't the license. It's about 200 workfiles, 15 direct-client phone numbers and 25 years of local adjustment knowledge, and the real exit barrier is fear of tail liability, not money. Solve the fear and the successor gets clients and know-how at near-zero acquisition cost. VCs assume AI will make appraisers obsolete. The near-term truth is that the supply of human signatures (the liability bearers) is collapsing faster than software replaces them, and whoever owns the signatures and the QC owns the workflow. Supervisors, not trainees, are the scarce resource.
first_30_days: Pull public state board rosters in 3-4 states (for example TX, OH, PA, CO) and filter certified residential appraisers licensed 25+ years. Run a free 'UAD 3.6: adapt or retire' session through local Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser Facebook groups. Sign 10 retirees to the $1,500 custody plus tail package. Recruit 5 trainees from local agents and inspectors. Hold two credit union lunches to line up the direct-client handoffs.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors.

title: Warranty Gap Desk for MEP Contractors
one_liner: Sell to the electrical and mechanical contractors who promise owners a warranty from substantial completion while their OEM warranties run from shipment or startup, and fund the service from the contractors' own warranty reserves.
customer: The warranty manager, contracts VP or CFO at mid-size to large electrical contractors, mechanical contractors and construction managers building data centers who furnish the MEP equipment themselves (colo, enterprise and neocloud jobs, not owner-furnished hyperscale). They give the owner a 12-24 month warranty and carry a warranty reserve on the balance sheet.
problem: The parent assumed the owner feels the pain. The party actually squeezed between two clocks is the contractor. The OEM warranty passes through on an OEM calendar (startup or 18 months from ship). The contractor's promise to the owner runs from substantial completion or Tier certification, and owner-side counsel are actively advising developers to push warranty commencement to certification (the law-firm guidance in the parent's evidence). Every month of delay widens the gap, and in that gap the contractor pays for defects out of pocket. Estimators price it as a flat percentage, project managers do not track it, and closeout binders bury the OEM terms. Contractor warranty reserves are real P&L items the CFO wants released, which gives a budget line the parent never had.
solution: 1) Bid-stage gap pricing. Read the subcontract warranty clause and the OEM quotes, compute gap-days by equipment line, and price it into the bid instead of a flat reserve. 2) Deferral riders on the contractor's own POs. A contractor buying hundreds of units per year has leverage the owner lacks, and the desk pools rider purchasing across contractor clients for discounts. 3) Pre-expiry proof test and claim filing on installed gear so the OEM, not the contractor, pays for defects (load-bank partner does the physical work). 4) Reserve-release package at contract end: a documented file showing what OEM claims were accepted and what exposure remains, so the CFO can release reserve early.
why_now: Owner counsel now push warranty starts to Tier certification while long-lead delivery and phase slippage stretch the shipment-to-certification interval. Data center MEP backlogs are large, so contractors have more warranty exposure on more sites than ever. Extraction of PO, contract and OEM terms into gap-days used to require a warranty analyst per job and is now nearly free.
revenue_model: Program fee per project, roughly 0.03-0.08% of MEP contract value (about $120-320K on a $400M scope), which is a small share of a typical reserve. Assumption to validate: reserves of around 0.5-2% of contract value. Plus 20% of OEM-accepted claims that would otherwise have been borne by the contractor. Plus a rider-pooling margin or referral fee from OEMs and rental partners. Renewals follow the contractor's project pipeline, so revenue is recurring across projects.
non_obvious_insight: The contractor is the only party in the chain holding an unhedged, quantifiable, budgeted warranty liability, and it is growing because of owner-side contract trends. Selling to the contractor also flips the leverage problem: one contractor buys from OEMs at volume, and a desk representing several contractors can win start-date deferrals that no single owner could. The buyer is a CFO with a reserve, not an owner's ops team with no budget.
first_30_days: Call 15 warranty managers and project executives at regional electrical and mechanical contractors with live data center work, sourced through NECA and MCAA chapters and surety brokers who track contractor exposures. Offer a free 'gap map' on two live projects using their subcontract warranty clause and OEM quotes. Target: three pilots at about $25K per project and one signed OEM rider negotiation. Confirm the key assumption early, which is what share of their data center equipment is contractor-furnished.
lineage: mutation of I0229 ('Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline. | How this version avoids them: Ethyco and Cx firms sell warranty-phase support to owners after occupancy; the buyer here is the contractor, and the pitch is reserve release, not deficiency documentation. Anyset and Nomic sell closeout compliance to GCs and owners (is the warranty in the binder, does it match spec), while this computes the gap between the OEM clock and the contractor's obligation, buys deferrals and files OEM claims. Equipment Warranty Log and DCIM tools track expiry dates with no gap logic. Wind end-of-warranty vendors and Sinovoltaics sell to owners of other asset classes. Trane's delayed-start rider is an input purchased at pooled volume. WCS serves equipment dealers, not construction contractors, and is a possible referral partner. Aggreko and Sunbelt Solomon are load-test suppliers. Because payment comes from the contractor's reserve, the collection problem of a 25-30% contingency on 'avoided cost' owed by an owner does not arise.

title: Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers
one_liner: Independent pharmacies hold the half of the PBM ledger that employers never see, which is what the PBM actually paid the pharmacy. Pool it to run spread audits for self-insured employers, and give pharmacies a stay-or-leave calculator for their take-it-or-leave-it PBM contracts.
customer: Two sides. First, independent pharmacies, at $99-199 a month for benchmarking and a network-contract modeler. Second, self-funded local employers, school districts, counties and union funds (from 100 to 5,000 lives), plus the benefit consultants and TPAs that serve them, who pay per audit or a share of verified savings.
problem: The employer sees only what it paid the PBM. The PBM sees both sides and hides one. The pharmacy sees what it was paid and what it paid the wholesaler, but has no benchmark and no idea whether the network offer that arrives every Q4 for January 1 is worse than its peers' terms. Everyone negotiates blind. PBMs threaten a pharmacy with losing about a quarter of its business if it declines, and a plan sponsor cannot verify 'pass-through' claims.
solution: Read-only ingestion of the pharmacy's 835 remittance files and invoice costs from its pharmacy management system (PMS). Output 1) per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement benchmarked against NADAC and an anonymized peer pool. 2) A stay-or-leave model of each 2027 network offer built from the pharmacy's own claims mix. 3) With sponsor consent, a claim-level tie-out of the pharmacy-paid amounts against the employer's PBM claims file. That yields a true spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member, delivered as an audit the employer can use to renegotiate or move to a transparent PBM.
why_now: The contract season for January 2027 is happening right now, which gives a hard deadline and a free entry wedge. Employer fiduciaries are under pressure from ERISA suits over PBM costs, state PBM transparency laws and FTC scrutiny. Pharmacy closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens closing about 1,200 stores) have given local officials political will. OCR and LLM parsing of messy remit PDFs now makes onboarding a one-day job rather than a consulting project.
revenue_model: Pharmacy subscription of $99-199 a month, or free in exchange for data. Employer audit fees of about $8k-25k per mid-size sponsor, or 10-20% of first-year verified savings. Data licenses to state employee plans, attorneys general, employer coalitions and consultants at a higher tier.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in the PBM fight holds half a ledger, and only the pharmacy can prove the gap. Thirty pharmacies in one county reconstruct the local school district's and county government's spread at claim level. Independents will hand this data over willingly because it is the first ammunition they have ever had against take-it-or-leave-it contracts.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 pharmacies through the state independent pharmacy association with the pitch 'we will model your 2027 PBM offers free'. Build parsers for the three biggest PBMs' remit formats (the 835 EDI standard helps). Deliver the first stay-or-leave reports. Hire a healthcare attorney to structure data-use terms, since provider-manual confidentiality clauses and HIPAA de-identification are the main risk. Offer one local school district or county a free pilot spread audit and turn the result into a one-page case study.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Truveris (truAudit / truGuard / Marketplace), Capital Rx (Judi Health), AffirmedRx, SmithRx. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I ran any query in this session. The verdict rests on direct fetches of about 20 competitor and source pages plus GitHub searches, not on a broad landscape scan. It is a provisional 'gap', not a confirmed one.

What I did not find: no company that ingests pharmacy-side remits, benchmarks per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement against a peer pool, models Q4 network offers, and ties pharmacy-paid amounts to an employer's PBM claims file. The employer-side audit market is served: Truveris, benefits consultants, and transparent PBMs that market pass-through. Their audits appear to start from what the PBM hands over, and I found no sign they hold the pharmacy-paid half.

The pharmacy-side gap is plausible. PioneerRx, PQS and CPESN pages show no reimbursement-benchmarking or contract-modeling feature. Not verified: pharmacy services administrative organizations (PSAOs such as Cardinal, AmerisourceBergen Elevate, AAP, Health Mart Atlas) and pharmacy management system vendors may already offer contract review or reimbursement reports to members. Confirm this in customer interviews before building, because the PSAOs negotiate PBM contracts and already hold members' remits.

The specific unserved wedge is a claim-level reconciliation between the pharmacy's actual paid amount and the employer's PBM claims file, delivered as a spread and rebate pass-through gap in dollars per member.

Risks that shrink the white space:
- PBM provider-manual confidentiality clauses and possible antitrust or information-exchange concerns when pooling competitors' reimbursement rates.
- Getting employer PBM claims files with sponsor consent.
- Pharmacy remits are not uniformly 835 files.
- The January 2027 contract window is roughly 3 months away and cannot be met by a product built from scratch.

title: Rotor Rescue: Scrapyard Magnet Pick-and-Pay
one_liner: A price-sheet-plus-gauss-meter program that pays scrapyards for magnet-dense motors and rotors they currently sell as steel and copper.
customer: Rare-earth magnet recyclers and magnet makers needing domestic recycled feed (they pay per kg with assay). Scrapyards, motor rebuilders and appliance/HVAC recyclers are the sellers.
problem: The rare-earth bottleneck is 'collection and disassembly rather than recovery chemistry.' Hard-drive magnet removal often costs more than the material is worth. Yards sell EV drive units, servo and elevator motors, and e-bike hub motors by copper and steel weight, and the NdFeB rotors go into the steel shred.
solution: Skip HDDs and target a short list of heavy, magnet-dense items. Yards get a phone app plus a $150 gauss meter that identifies magnet-bearing units and shows a payout per unit or per rotor. A mobile pull cell or the yard's own labor removes rotors. We aggregate and assay them, then sell a certified, traceable magnet-feed stream to recyclers.
why_now: The IEA puts China at about 90% of material recovery capacity. The DoD-MP deal and the Texas magnet campus create domestic pull, and DOE announced $134M for critical-mineral demonstrations in June 2026. Recyclers such as Cyclic Materials and IonicRE are funded and need feed.
revenue_model: Spread between the recycler's price per kg of assayed magnet feed and the yard payout plus pull cost. Optional premium for defense-traceable lots. Small SaaS fee for the identification and price app.
non_obvious_insight: Rare-earth economics fail on tiny magnets (HDDs) but work on a few heavy items. No one publishes a price by motor model, so yards do not know a rotor holds hundreds of grams to kilograms of NdFeB. Price discovery is the missing product, not a new chemistry.

title: GLP-1 Palate Panel for Food R&D
one_liner: A managed panel of GLP-1 users and their households that food and restaurant companies rent to test products, portions and health claims.
customer: R&D and insights teams at mid-size CPG (protein, snacks, frozen), restaurant chain menu teams, foodservice for hospitals and senior living, and supplement brands that need claim substantiation ($25-150k per study).
problem: 73% of GLP-1 users report taste changes and 70% lose joy in eating, so 'just add protein' fails. About 70% change what the household eats, and non-users adopt 30-50% of the changes, so the affected base is ~50% larger than the user count. Food companies are reformulating and launching 'GLP-1 friendly' labels on general-population panels and conflicting forecasts.
solution: Recruit and maintain a segmented panel (drug, dose, weeks on therapy, aversion profile, household makeup). Run sensory, portion and format tests plus home-use tests and 8-12 week muscle and satiety claim studies. Deliver 'aversion maps' (which textures and smells trigger nausea at which dose) and household spillover models.
why_now: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled from ~11% to 22% in under 3 years. Pills launched in 2026 broaden the base. CPG is mid-reformulation, and FTC claim scrutiny makes 'evidence-backed' labels valuable. Purchase-panel incumbents see what is bought, not why.
revenue_model: $25-150k per study, plus $40-100k/year data subscription for 'aversion map' updates.
non_obvious_insight: The 'GLP-1 consumer' is 5-6 sensory segments that shift with dose and week on therapy, not one persona. Forecasting from sales data cannot separate them, but a panel can. The picks-and-shovels of a reformulation wave are the testers, not the brands.
first_30_days: Recruit 300 panelists from subreddits and Facebook groups with a $25 incentive, verified by photo of the pharmacy label. Publish a free 'taste change' survey report for press. Cold-email 30 CPG insights leads and land a first paid pilot of about $25k.
