title: Coder-Signed Reasonable-Value Reports for Injury Defense
one_liner: A 48-hour, coder-certified benchmark report that tells defense lawyers and auto carriers what a letter-of-protection medical bill is actually worth.
customer: Insurance defense law firms and auto-carrier litigation/SIU units handling bodily-injury claims in tort-reform states (Florida, Georgia, Texas, Louisiana first). Volume firms pay per report. Carriers pay monthly.
problem: Plaintiff-side injury cases increasingly rest on treatment provided under letters of protection (LOP), where the provider is paid from the settlement and bills at a private rate card. Defense lawyers have to show what the care is really worth. Today that means a $3-5k billing expert, a slow turnaround, and a fight over methodology. Most claims examiners cannot read a CMS-1500 or UB-04, so inflated bills mostly get paid or settled at face value.
solution: Intake the itemized bill and records. Map every line to CPT/HCPCS and revenue codes and flag unbundling (e.g. 99215-25 plus separate injection administration, physician-owned ASC facility fees stacked on the professional fee, stacked imaging reads). Benchmark each line against Medicare multiples, hospital-posted commercial negotiated rates from price-transparency files, and local percentiles. The output is a Daubert-hardened PDF signed by a certified coder (CPC/CCS) with an optional expert declaration or testimony upsell. It is a methodology plus a template, so the marginal cost per report is about an hour of coder time.
why_now: Florida's 2023 tort reform made LOP arrangements discoverable and admitted evidence of amounts actually paid. Georgia's 2025 tort reform pushed similar rules, and other states are copying. Hospital price-transparency rules that took full effect in 2026 now require actual payment amounts where rates are percentages or algorithms, so a defensible local benchmark exists for the first time.
revenue_model: $295-$695 per report. Expert declaration or testimony at $1,500-$3,500. $2-5k/month subscriptions for carriers and volume firms with a report quota. Gross margin is high because coders are paid per report as contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Inside a hospital, chargemaster prices are understood to be fiction, and every biller knows what things really get paid. Injury lawyers have been arguing about 'reasonable value' without that insider map. Certified coders also know the tells of bills built for litigation rather than payment: modifier-25 patterns, unbundled facility fees, and E/M levels that no insurer would ever pay. The market is starved of people credentialed and willing to say so on paper. The moat is a coder bench plus a methodology that survives cross-examination, not software.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-5 CPC/CCS coders (ex-hospital, remote, contractors) and one defense-attorney advisor to review the methodology memo. Build the report template from the free Medicare fee schedules plus a few metro-area price-transparency files. Cold-email about 100 Florida and Georgia defense firms and claims managers, and offer 5 free reports on live cases in exchange for a methodology review and a testimonial. Convert the first 3-5 to $349 per report, then price the expert declaration as an add-on.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Enlyte (Mitchell/Genex) Demand Package Review and Bodily Injury Integrated Solutions, FAIR Health, EvenUp, Turquoise Health. White space: Caveat: the WebSearch budget hit its cap (200 of 200) before I could run the planned searches on startups, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and forums. This verdict rests on direct page fetches only. Treat 'gap' as provisional. Before building, someone should spend an hour on the searches I could not run: 'letter of protection medical bill review', 'reasonable value expert Florida LOP', and Crunchbase/YC for 'LOP' or 'defense medical bill'.

What I could confirm: no vendor I could reach sells a fixed-fee (about $300-700), fast-turnaround, coder-certified report with an optional declaration or testimony upsell aimed at LOP reasonable value. The nearest product is Enlyte's Demand Package Review. It is a carrier-side workflow product with nurse and analyst review at 3-4 to 10 days. It shows no coder signature, no LOP framing and no testimony. It also lacks the piece defense lawyers need most, which is a signed opinion that survives cross-examination. Data companies (FAIR Health, Turquoise) sell inputs, not signed opinions. EvenUp is plaintiff-side.

Specific white space: (1) small and mid-size defense firms and panel counsel who can't justify a $3-5k expert on a $30-100k claim. (2) Coder-signed output that holds up under cross-examination, tied to the LOP disclosure record. (3) States without a statutory benchmark, where reasonable value is contested.

Two weaknesses in the pitch. (a) Florida is partly commoditized by statute. Fla. Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. A large part of the Florida 'report' is therefore a Medicare-multiple calculation from free CMS files, which a claims shop or existing vendor could copy quickly. (b) The hospital price-transparency 'why now' is weaker than the idea claims. CMS says enforcement of the new rules starts April 1, 2026 (https://www.cms.gov/priorities/key-initiatives/hospital-price-transparency). But LOP care is mostly delivered by chiropractors, pain clinics, orthopedic groups and physician-owned ASCs, not hospitals. I inferred that from how LOP cases usually work and did not verify it. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files.

title: Neutral Ground Baseline for Foundation Projects
one_liner: A developer-paid, two-sided satellite baseline of every neighboring tower, delivered at the same time to neighbors and insurers, and sold as a line item by the geotech and vibration-monitoring firms already on the job.
customer: Payer: mid-size South Florida condo developers and general contractors (and their deep-foundation subcontractors) on projects with pile-driving, dewatering or deep excavation within about 300 m of occupied towers. Co-buyers: builders-risk and CGL underwriters, MGAs and wholesale brokers who insure those projects. Channel: geotech and vibration-monitoring engineering firms who already write the monitoring plan and can resell.
problem: Neighbor claims are the tail risk of urban high-rise foundation work. Vibration and settlement claims, injunction threats and stop-work fights can add months of construction-loan carry on a $150M-$400M tower. The developer's own crack survey is discounted as self-serving. Underwriters have no independent evidence of pre-existing condition, so they price the whole neighborhood as worst case, or add sublimits, higher deductibles or exclusions for adjacent-property damage. The UM study showed many towers were already sinking at mm/yr for reasons unrelated to any neighbor. Developers cannot prove that, and neither can anyone else.
solution: Neighbor Ledger. At permit or early foundation stage, process the archive for every building in the influence zone (typically 15-40 towers) and issue a neutral baseline package. It goes the same day to (a) the developer and its insurer and (b) each neighboring association through a read-only portal. Neighbors get a free 3-page report on their own tower, which gives them evidence and a reason to stop fighting the permit. Timestamps and data hashes are anchored, so neither side can dispute the record. During construction, a monthly delta report flags any tower whose motion departs from its own trend or from control towers. When a claim is filed, a dispute packet is generated within days. A rule is written into every contract: the company gives identical data to both sides and never testifies for either. Expert work goes to an independent geodesist panel. Priced fixed per project and sold as an add-on line item on the geotech firm's monitoring contract.
why_now: Miami's high-rise foundation boom is running against an unusually alert neighbor base: the 2024 UM study was widely covered, Marenas spent about $20K on sensors after a neighbor started work, and the Estructura June 2026 campaign has associations asking developers for data. Post-Surfside underwriters demand structural documentation, and softening reinsurance capacity makes MGAs hungry for differentiated loss-control tools. Processing cost has collapsed with free OPERA DISP-S1, Sentinel-1 and NISAR data.
revenue_model: $18K baseline per project at permit, plus $2.5K/month during foundation and superstructure phases (about 18 months), so about $60-65K per project against a $150M+ build. Reseller share of 20-25% to the geotech or vibration firm. Insurers and MGAs get a portfolio loss-control dashboard as a $25-50K/year program license, in exchange for a premium credit or a warranty requiring the ledger. Assumed 30-40 new high-rise foundation starts per year across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach (verify from permit data), so about 12 projects in year one at roughly $700K. Expansion to Tampa, Orlando and Houston follows once insurers accept it.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's flaw was that boards may not want to know. Here the party with the strongest need to know is the developer, whose worst nightmare is a false or mistaken damage claim. A baseline showing the neighbor was already sinking is worth more to the developer than to the neighbor. Neutrality is the product: one record both sides accepted is worth more than two competing reports, the way an escrow agent is worth more than two lawyers. Because every competitor is on one side, refusing to take a side is a position none of them can copy without losing their existing clients. Once about 10 projects and two insurers rely on ledgers, a city or county can make a settlement baseline a permit condition, as some European cities require for deep excavation next to older buildings. That would turn a product into infrastructure (hedge: verify local precedent).
first_30_days: Week 1: list the 6-8 geotech and vibration-monitoring firms with active Miami-Dade or Broward jobs, using their public monitoring plans and permit files. Build unsolicited Neighbor Ledgers for 5 currently active sites from free data. Week 2: pitch each firm 'add this as a line item, you keep 25%, we do all the work.' Meet 4 builders-risk and CGL wholesale brokers and MGAs with a one-page loss-control pitch and one question: would you give a premium credit or require it? Weeks 3-4: close one developer pilot at half price ($9K) on a site in early foundation stage, in exchange for an underwriter introduction, and sign one geotech reseller. Kill test: if no geotech firm will bundle it and no underwriter will credit it, drop the model.

title: UK Vet Price Panel for Investors and Insurers
one_liner: The first normalized, ownership-linked, time-series panel of UK vet prices, built from the price lists the CMA now forces every practice to publish, and licensed as a data feed to equity and credit investors, pet insurers and independent-practice bodies.
customer: Three payers with different budgets. (1) Buy-side and sell-side analysts and credit or private-equity funds with exposure to listed and sponsor-owned vet consolidators (CVS Group, Pets at Home/Vets4Pets, IVC Evidensia, Medivet, VetPartners, Linnaeus). (2) Pricing, claims and panel-strategy heads at UK pet insurers and their reinsurers. (3) Independent-practice trade bodies such as FIVP, which need to benchmark independents against groups. The first buyer to target is the analyst covering CVS Group, because alt-data budgets are large and the purchase decision is one person.
problem: Consolidators keep local practice brands after acquisition, so almost no one can build a clean same-practice, before-and-after price series by owner. The CMA found consolidated practices had about 5% higher claim values and 9.2% higher prices within four years, but insurers, lenders and analysts still cannot track drift by group or postcode. Insurers hold itemised claim lines but no market panel to compare them to. Investors underwrite price-led same-store growth with anecdotes. The official RCVS comparison data will not reach approved third parties until late 2027.
solution: Crawl and normalize the published price lists monthly, keeping history. The CMA order requires 36 standard items across six patient categories (216 prices per practice), written estimates over GBP 500, itemised bills, and ownership disclosure. Map each practice to its ultimate owner using the mandated ownership statements, Companies House and the RCVS register. Deliver: (a) a monthly group-level price index and same-practice change series, (b) a practice-level API with postcode reference ranges, (c) an alert feed when a group re-prices a category. Extension beyond the 36 routine items: insurers contribute itemised estimate and invoice lines above GBP 500 in exchange for a discount, which extends the panel to orthopaedics, oncology and emergency work. Apply to become an RCVS approved third party the day that channel opens, so the RCVS feed becomes an input rather than a threat. US extension later from insurer-contributed claim lines.
why_now: The CMA's final report (March 2026) became an order with RCVS undertakings accepted on 22 September 2026. Large groups' first transparency duties start 23 December 2026, and smaller practices follow through 2027. RCVS's enhanced Find a Vet is due by 22 June 2027, with business data supply later in 2027 and sharing with third parties under restrictions. That gives a 9-12 month window in which a normalized, owner-linked panel from the start of publication is the only structured source, and history cannot be back-filled later. Cheap LLM extraction handles the mess of 5,000 differently formatted price pages.
revenue_model: Data licences. Investor feed at GBP 30-60k a year. Insurer and reinsurer feed at GBP 20-50k, with a 40-50% discount for contributing itemised claim lines. Trade-body and independent-practice benchmarking at GBP 5-15k. Month-12 target of about GBP 550-600k ARR from 8 funds at 45k, 6 insurers at 30k and 3 bodies at 15k. Marginal cost is close to zero after the crawler exists. Year-2 upside comes from extending to US insurers' claim lines (US premiums grew about 19% in 2025) and to dental and specialty procedures.
non_obvious_insight: The CMA did not only mandate price disclosure. It mandated ownership disclosure, and that is the join key nobody had. A price series linked to owner is worth far more to an investor than a price list is to a pet owner, so the buyer with the deepest pocket is not the insurer or the consumer. The panel is also a cornered resource in time: every month a rival waits is history they can never buy. The parent's canonical-code thesis still holds, because regulation just created the first common procedure list and this business maps to it before anyone else. Insurers' claim lines then extend that list into severity territory that the 36 routine items cannot reach.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build crawlers for the six largest groups' price pages and 300 independents, and load the 36-item by six-category schema. Many practices already publish some prices ahead of the deadline. Days 10-20: build the ownership graph from the mandated ownership statements, Companies House and the RCVS register. Publish a free Pre-Order Baseline note on group price levels to draw inbound from analysts and journalists. Days 20-30: pitch 15 named buyers (5 analysts covering CVS Group and Pets at Home, 5 credit or PE funds with vet exposure, 5 insurer pricing heads) on a founding-subscriber annual deal at GBP 24k with a price lock and input on the index. Target 3 signed letters of intent by day 60 and the first live index the week after 23 December 2026.
lineage: mutation of I1056 ('Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: VetControl (Illingen, Germany), Five Sigma (Clive AI claims adjuster), Sirma (custom ML for PetsBest, now under Synchrony), FairVet. White space: Nobody I found sells a US, insurer-facing, explainable edit library (canonical line-item codes, bundling and duplicate rules, unit plausibility, reason codes) with cross-carrier benchmarks, to mid-size MGAs and TPAs.

- VetControl is the only true direct analog, and it is German, GOT-based, a services-plus-software hybrid, and shows no US customers.
- Five Sigma and Sirma classify line items for coverage, not for pricing or bundling.
- FairVet and Vet Receipt hold consumer-sourced benchmark data with no insurer-grade normalization.
- Trupanion and Lassie built in-house and are not customers.

The demand evidence is indirect: cost inflation, plus vendors like VetControl selling a similar product in Germany. | How this version avoids them: FairVet and Vet Receipt are US consumer bill-upload tools with thin, crowd-sourced data and no ownership graph, and neither sells institutional time series. Vet Price Comparison (UK) is a consumer directory, and RCVS Find a Vet is by design a directory rather than a league table, arrives mid-2027 and later becomes an input. AAHA's fee reference is a US survey, not a price panel. VetControl is German invoice verification for insurers and does not do UK market panels. Verisk's pet program is US policy and rating only. Trupanion and Lassie are in-house insurers and not customers, and UK insurers could scrape themselves but lack the cross-group history, the ownership join and neutral positioning. Selling to investors avoids the parent's balance-bill and vet-fight risk entirely, and the price index never reduces a policyholder's claim.

title: Grid-Readiness Model Audit for Data Center Lenders
one_liner: An independent checker for private-credit funds, banks and delay-in-start-up insurers that audits a borrower's large-load models and ride-through evidence and gives an energization-risk opinion, the same way financial-model auditors already serve project-finance lenders.
customer: Data center and GPU-cloud finance teams at credit funds, banks and ABS arrangers, plus the lender's independent engineers, technical advisors and project-finance law firms that act as the channel. Delay-in-start-up (DSU) insurers and MGAs are the second payer. The borrower's fee is paid at lender direction, which is the market norm for lender advisors.
problem: Lenders finance billions of dollars of campuses and GPU fleets. Interest accrues and hardware depreciates while the site waits for energization. Their diligence covers construction cost, schedule, MEP and offtake, but grid dynamic behavior is a black box authored by an interested party: the borrower's own consultant says interconnection is on track. After the 2024 Northern Virginia load-loss event and ERCOT's new rules, lenders have no independent way to judge whether the load model will pass, whether ride-through settings will trip the site, or how far energization could slip. Developer-side consultants such as Electranix and Danovo are conflicted, and the lender's independent engineer typically lacks EMT skills.
solution:
Sell a check, not a build.
1) A pre-close Grid-Readiness Opinion of $30-75k per site. It is an independent review of the borrower's PSS/E and EMT models, study reports, interconnection-agreement conditions and UPS, PSU and firmware settings against the ISO's rules and generic reference models. It ends with a red/amber/green rating and a P50/P90 energization-slip range.
2) A conditions-precedent and covenant kit for law firms: draw conditions such as ISO-accepted model, passed ride-through test and firmware freeze.
3) Re-attestation of $10-20k whenever GPU generation or UPS firmware changes, triggered by covenant.
4) A portfolio dashboard for lenders by ISO and site, and an anonymized risk dataset for DSU underwriters.
Analysts run rule-based checklists and scripted checks through the PSS/E Python API, so each review takes about 40-80 hours. Our own modeling is never required.
why_now: Neocloud and data center debt (delayed-draw term loans, GPU-backed facilities, ABS) grew explosively in 2025-26, and energization delay has become a visible schedule risk in publicly reported neocloud results. Regulatory rules that make models and ride-through a gating item are now in force in Texas, with PJM and NERC large-load work following. Lenders and insurers are looking for a diligence item to price, and nobody offers it yet.
revenue_model: Borrower-paid, lender-directed fees of $30-75k per site per financing and $10-20k per refresh re-attestation. DSU insurers pay $10-25k per underwriting review, or a data license, and later take a share of premium through an MGA program. Rough bottom-up: 200 qualifying US financings a year (assumption to verify) at $50k is about $10M, and 400 sites refreshed at $15k is about $6M, so this is a $15-25M niche. It is a thin, high-margin analyst business that later becomes a rating or registry.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer of a grid model is whoever bears the cost of delay, not the grid. Project finance already has an independent-checker culture, with financial-model audits and independent engineers, because lenders will not trust numbers authored by the borrower. A dynamic load model is the same kind of black-box spreadsheet driving a billion-dollar decision. The parent's three structural threats become tailwinds here. Free EPRI or NERC generic models become the benchmark we audit against. OEM secrecy is irrelevant because we test the borrower's model against acceptance criteria and measured behavior and need no OEM IP. title: Auto Loan-End Event Exchange for Add-On Refunds
one_liner: Start by recovering unearned add-on refunds on repossessed and charged-off loans for small lenders on pure contingency (cash the lender itself keeps), then turn those lender-attested loan-end events into a neutral exchange that administrators, carriers and regulators plug into, so refunds become a statutory event pushed to the administrator instead of a claim the borrower must pull.
customer: Stage 1: collections and recovery managers at credit unions and community banks with $200M to $3B in auto loans (too small for in-house recovery teams), plus the collection agencies and recovery BPOs that serve them. Stage 2 payers: GAP and service-contract administrators and their fronting or contractual-liability carriers and reinsurers; regulators get free access. Governance: founding lenders receive equity or rebates through a cooperative structure such as a CUSO.
problem: At repossession or charge-off, the unearned refund on financed GAP, service contracts and other add-ons is collectible cash for the lender and shrinks the deficiency billed to the member. Small lenders rarely chase it because each administrator has its own paper process and the dealer chargeback fight breeds stalling. The deeper failure is informational: where a state requires automatic refunds on payoff (the parent cites New Jersey; verify), the administrator cannot comply because nobody tells it the loan ended. No one sits between the lender who knows and the administrator who owes, so every refund is a bilateral fight with no shared standard, no SLA and no scoreboard.
solution: Stage 1, sellable within 6 months, is a Repo Refund Desk. The lender drops a monthly file of repossessions and charge-offs plus contract images (secure upload, no core integration). The system reads the add-ons, matches administrators, computes refunds by state rule, files cancellations under the lender's assignment of unearned premiums, and tracks to payment. Refunds post to the lender's loan account, cutting both the write-off and the member's deficiency. Fee: 20 to 25% of cash actually recovered, nothing upfront. Stage 2: every processed case becomes a signed loan-end event (VIN, contract ID, event type, date, products, computed refund). Publish an open Loan-End Event schema and API; administrators get structured, lender-attested cancellation requests in their own intake format, cheaper than manual intake and a defensible statutory trigger. Payoff and total-loss events join (the parent's payoff-desk plug-in becomes a free module). Stage 3: carriers and reinsurers get true early-termination curves and refund-SLA dashboards; regulators get a free supervisory view; later a settlement layer and a refund-advance facility.
why_now: Record subprime delinquency and roughly 3M repossessions a year create a large event flow today. 84-month loans mean add-ons are unearned at almost every repossession. LLM contract reading cuts per-case processing from tens of dollars to cents, which is what makes contingency pricing work. State regulators and private plaintiffs are filling a federal enforcement retreat (verify), raising the value of an audit trail. Core-processor API marketplaces and CUSOs make plug-in distribution to credit unions cheaper than a direct sales force (verify).
revenue_model: Stage 1: 20 to 25% contingency on recovered cash. Illustration to validate in the free retrospective audit: a lender with $1B in auto loans, about 1,000 repossessions a year, 45% with financed add-ons, about $700 average unearned, 60% currently unclaimed is roughly $190K of new cash a year and a $40K to $47K annual fee. Stage 2: administrators pay $2 to $5 per attested event plus a compliance subscription; carriers and reinsurers pay $50K to $250K a year for termination and SLA data; regulators free. Stage 3: a 0.5 to 1% network fee on refunds settled through the exchange, and a refund-advance facility funded with outside capital. Stage 1 alone is a viable small business; the exchange is the venture-scale option.
non_obvious_insight: The stalling problem is less about willingness than information: nobody tells the administrator the loan ended, and the one party that knows, the lender, has never had a reason to say so. Refund-on-repossession, unlike refund-on-payoff, is the lender's own cash, so the lender pays willingly, and the same act produces the signed events that convert each administrator's private float into a scoreboarded, regulator-visible liability. The exchange's real asset is the true early-termination rate for financed add-ons, which no administrator, reinsurer or regulator can observe today because they see only claimed cancellations, not loans that actually ended. That number prices and reserves every GAP and service-contract program.
first_30_days: Weeks 1 to 2: build administrator playbooks for the 20 largest administrators and 10 states (as in the parent) and the pro-rata engine. Weeks 1 to 3: offer 5 credit unions or community banks a free retrospective audit of their last 12 months of repossessions and charge-offs and report the cash left on the table. Weeks 3 to 4: sign 2 on 25% contingency and process live cases weekly; recruit one collection agency or recovery BPO as a reseller. In parallel, publish Loan-End Event schema v0.1 openly, and send an SLA-scoreboard mockup built from the first 100 cases to compliance heads at 10 administrators and consumer-services staff at 2 state insurance departments. Target: $25K of recovered cash logged, 3 lender LOIs, 1 administrator willing to receive structured requests.

title: Contractor-First Road Billing, Then Repair Lending
one_liner: Invert the parent: sell to plow and gravel contractors who each serve dozens of handshake roads with a get-paid rail that binds every household to its share, then use the payment history and recorded covenants to become the lender for culvert and washout repairs no bank will touch.
customer: Wedge: independent plow, gravel and excavation contractors serving 15-80 private roads and shared driveways each, starting in one snow-belt county in Maine or NH. Later payers: road associations as borrowers, and community banks, credit unions and CDFIs as capital partners who buy participations in the loans we originate and service.
problem: A contractor plows a 12-home road on a verbal 'we'll split it'. He bills one neighbor, who fronts the money and chases the others. After one or two free-riders the fronting neighbor quits, so the contractor drops the road or absorbs the loss. Contractors also front fuel, labor and equipment for a season and are paid unevenly. When a culvert or bridge fails, a $30-150k repair has no borrower, since there is no entity, no assets and no financials. NC's post-Helene program (verified) demanded a 50% cost share, a single point of contact and proof of ownership, so roads that could not front cash and had no organization were shut out. Both sides of the road are cash-starved for the same reason, which is no legal counterparty.
solution: Phase 1, sold this October to be live by first snow. RoadPay for contractors: the contractor enters a road's seasonal price. Each household receives an e-sign Road Service Agreement (pro-rata formula, driveway-level opt-in, dispute rule) with autopay via Stripe Connect direct charges, so we never hold funds. The contractor gets one dashboard across all roads, automatic reminders and statements, and monthly payouts. Phase 2, winter: Season Advance. We advance 60-80% of a signed road's seasonal contract to the contractor, funded by a small credit line, and repay ourselves from the households' autopay through April. We underwrite at the road level using percent of households on autopay, contractor history and driveway geometry. Phase 3, year 2: Graduation. Roads with two clean seasons are invited to record an assessment-lien covenant (through the closing-rescue-style formation service), because it lowers their borrowing rate. Phase 4: Repair and cost-share bridge loans. $25-150k loans to the association for culverts, regrading and bridge repairs, repaid over 5-10 years from assessments, funded by CDFI and community-bank participation with us as originator and servicer. The same facility can bridge the up-front 50% of state reimbursement programs.
why_now: Winter 2026-27 seasonal contracts get signed in October and November, about six weeks from today. That gives a hard deadline and a full season of data inside a six-month window. Embedded payments are now a commodity (Stripe Connect handles onboarding, split payouts and money-movement compliance), which is the Wardley shift that makes a two-person team viable. Post-Helene aid design (verified) teaches that organized counterparties get capital and unorganized roads do not. Document extraction makes reading recorded covenants cheap enough to underwrite each road. Contractor cost inflation since 2021 plausibly makes non-payment more painful (hypothesis to test in interviews).
revenue_model: Phase 1: 4% of billings collected, paid by the contractor (no per-household fee, so the PayHOA $2 anchor never applies). Phase 2: 3-5% fee on advances, turned several times per season. Phase 4: 2-3% origination plus about 1.5% servicing on loans sold to bank partners, plus net interest on any retained slice. Illustration: 100 contractors x 40 roads x $3,000 is about $12M of billings, so about $480k of rail revenue. If 5% of roads borrow $60k a year, that is about $12M of loans and roughly $300-500k of origination and servicing. Early revenue is small. The business becomes large only if the payment history and lien-backed collateral become the standard underwriting file for private roads, which is the 10x claim.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the best data and the strongest incentive is the contractor, not the neighbors. He knows every road's parcels, who pays, and which culvert is about to fail, and one phone call reaches 40 roads. His invoice is a high-frequency touchpoint neighbors already accept, whereas a formation package is a rare, compliance-flavored purchase. The legal entity stops being a product and becomes collateral. Neighbors will sign a recorded covenant to cut their repair loan rate from, say, 14% to 8%, which they would never do for 'compliance'. It also removes the parent's conflict of interest, since the contractor is the customer rather than a party we take a procurement fee from.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 plow and gravel contractors in one county through local snow-removal and excavation groups, feed and hardware stores and Facebook groups, and offer free first-season setup on their 3 most annoying roads. Have an attorney spend $2-4k reviewing a generic Road Service Agreement and consumer-ACH disclosures. Build a no-code MVP in 2 weeks (contractor form, e-sign page, Stripe Connect autopay, manual reconciliation sheet). Convert at least 25 roads before first snow and measure the household sign rate (target 75% or better), autopay success and contractor willingness to pay 4%. Open a conversation with one CDFI or community credit union about a $250k participation for advances. Riskiest assumptions: whether households sign a contractor-issued agreement, and how to handle free-riders on a shared road, since the contractor can skip non-signers' driveways but not the common road. Also confirm lending and money-transmission licensing with counsel before Phase 2.

title: Stack-Pooled 24/7 Article 14 Desk for Non-EU Brands
one_liner: A guaranteed-SLA Assigned Representative that files CRA Article 14 reports for 50-250 person non-EU connected-device brands, doing the triage once per shared component stack (Tuya, ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek) and fanning it out to every client on that stack.
customer: Medium-sized (50-250 staff, above the small-enterprise fine exemption) non-EU smart-home, e-mobility and networking brands based in Shenzhen, Taiwan, Korea and the US that sell into the EU via Amazon EU and retail. Their firmware comes from an ODM on one of 3 shared stacks: Tuya/Matter modules, ESP-IDF/ESP32, or OpenWrt/Realtek SDKs. The buyer is the head of product or compliance; the introduction comes through the EU Responsible Person/EPR (WEEE and packaging) service providers who already serve these sellers.
problem: These brands do not know what is inside their own firmware because the ODM built it, so they cannot tell whether a KEV/EUVD entry hits them. They have no one awake in Europe at 3am Sunday to decide 'actively exploited, affects us, file'. The 72h and 14-day clocks carry fines even if the 24h clock does not, and their EU retail partners will start asking for proof of process. Existing options each miss part of this. Software (CVD Portal, CRACI, Regulus) stops at timers and drafts, with filing left to the customer. Finite State and H-X draft notices but leave filing to the customer. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 or price. EcoComply is an AR mandate with no triage.
solution: Three things in one contract. (1) Named-analyst AR mandate plus a written SLA: triage decision within 4h and early warning filed inside 24h, weekends included, under a client-approved decision tree and pre-authorised actions. (2) Stack-pooled triage: a stack owner analyses each exploited entry once against the stack's component graph and issues per-firmware-version pre-approved VEX and notice drafts to every enrolled brand on that stack, so a client-named analyst only checks the version delta and files. (3) Firmware-fingerprint onboarding: the brand uploads a firmware image or OTA URL and the desk builds the component list itself, removing the missing-SBOM problem. Every KEV/EUVD entry also gets a timestamped per-product 'affected / not affected' decision, delivered monthly as a signed monitoring evidence log. That log is the recurring deliverable when nothing was exploited, and it is what retailers and market surveillance authorities will ask for. The 24h and 72h drills run on the client's own stack.
why_now: Article 14 reporting went live on 11 Sep 2026 (about 18 days ago) and the ENISA SRP opened the same day. Patchstack shows managed filing is now legal and being productised, so the window before it becomes a checkbox is roughly 6-12 months. Retail supplier manuals are being rewritten for the Dec 2027 full application, and GPSR (since Dec 2024) already trained these sellers to buy EU-representative services.
revenue_model: Base fee of about EUR 3.6-4.8k per year per product family (AR mandate, stack monitoring, monthly evidence log, one drill), well above EcoComply's EUR 1.5k AR-only anchor but below a monthly PSIRT retainer. Filing events cost EUR 1.5-3k each. Tabletop drills and 'clock audit' are EUR 1.5-5k. Wholesale white-label 24/7 back-end capacity is sold to TUV, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas, TridentSec and SBOM platforms. Target is 100 product families by month 12 (about EUR 400k ARR). One stack analyst covering 30-100 clients keeps gross margin above 65%.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not filing, it is the stack-to-firmware truth table. Brands do not know what is inside, but the desk sees which SDK forks and versions actually ship across dozens of brands. That is a cornered resource that a one-off consultancy cannot copy: each new client on a stack has near-zero marginal analyst cost and improves the fingerprint coverage. Also, 95% of what the desk produces is 'not affected'. Selling signed negative evidence as the monthly deliverable fixes the judges' 'insurance nobody buys until audited' flaw. Targeting 50-250 person firms sidesteps the Art 64(10) small-enterprise exemption on the 24h fine.
first_30_days: Week 1: get a professional-indemnity quote, and get written confirmation from ENISA or a national CSIRT that an external firm can serve as AR using personal EU Login accounts. Get counsel to settle how the 24h clock starts when the desk detects first, and draft the AR mandate and decision tree. Weeks 1-2: build component graphs for 3 stacks (ESP-IDF, OpenWrt/Realtek, Tuya) covering the top 25 exploited component families of the last 24 months, using open-source firmware unpacking such as EMBA. Weeks 2-4: sell a EUR 1.5k '24h drill + firmware fingerprint' to 20 brands sourced from 3 EPR/GPSR representative providers and Amazon-EU seller communities. Contract 3 part-time named analysts across time zones and confirm the SRP login rules apply to them.
